text: This is the last lesson in the path. What you put in front of a hiring manager, and how you answer the questions this exact project is likely to draw, matters as much as the project itself.

A portfolio entry isn't the full GitHub link and nothing else. It's a one-paragraph problem statement in your own words, the architecture diagram from Lesson 2, two or three real code snippets that show judgment -- the CALCULATE-filtered MRR measure, not a plain SELECT star -- the repo link with a README, and a link to or screenshot of the actual dashboard, the single most convincing piece of evidence this is a finished, working platform.

This project draws specific questions by component. On dbt: walk me through your staging-to-marts layering. On Airflow: why does your DAG wait for both loads before running dbt. On security: what's the difference between RBAC and masking. On the numbers: how do you know your MRR is actually correct -- that last one is worth preparing for specifically.

A confident, specific answer -- I'd check Airflow's run history first, then dbt test results, then query history -- demonstrates more seniority than any amount of DAX or SQL fluency alone. And this course's own Resource Vault and Worked Examples are evidence too: a written troubleshooting checklist and worked examples extending the project is a concrete answer to how you keep learning beyond a course.
That's the full Snowflake Data Engineering Capstone -- Snowflake, dbt, Airflow, Power BI, Git, and Terraform, tied into one platform you can actually talk through.
